title: Numbers 7:12–47
context: The first six days of the altar’s dedication record the gifts of Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Reuben, Simeon, and Gad, following the order of the camp in Numbers 2. Each leader brings exactly the same gift: silver vessels with a grain offering, a gold ladle of incense, and animals for burnt, sin, and peace offerings. The repetition gives every tribe the same full record, so that no tribe’s gift is summarized or passed over.

verses.text: He who offered his offering the first day was Nahshon the son of Amminadab, of the tribe of Judah,
verses.arminianNotes: Judah goes first, matching its place at the head of the eastern camp (Numbers 2:3). Nahshon later appears in David’s genealogy (Ruth 4:20). Arminian readers see leadership exercised by example. Both traditions note Judah’s prominence anticipated in Genesis 49:10.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Judah’s precedence fits God’s purposes for the royal line, and Matthew 1:4 places Nahshon among Jesus’ ancestors. Shared ground: the first gift comes from the tribe through which the promised King will come.

verses.text: and his offering was: one silver platter, the weight of which was one hundred thirty shekels, one silver bowl of seventy shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a meal offering;
verses.arminianNotes: The silver platter (about 1.3 kilograms, per the WEB footnote on the shekel) and bowl hold fine flour mixed with oil for a meal offering (Leviticus 2). Arminian readers see costly devotion offered freely. Both traditions note the standard sanctuary shekel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the vessels are weighed by the sanctuary shekel, a fixed standard set by God, not the giver. Shared ground: the meal offering presents the fruit of labor to God.

verses.text: one golden ladle of ten shekels, full of incense;
verses.arminianNotes: The gold ladle, about 100 grams, is full of incense. Incense is linked with prayer elsewhere in Scripture (Psalm 141:2). Arminian readers see prayer and worship rising to God. Both traditions agree that incense was offered only as God prescribed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that incense must follow God’s command, as Leviticus 10:1–2 showed. The gold marks its use near the holy place. Shared ground: incense symbolizes worship and prayer offered to God.

verses.text: one young bull, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering;
verses.arminianNotes: A young bull, a ram, and a year-old lamb are offered as a burnt offering, wholly consumed on the altar (Leviticus 1). Arminian readers see total devotion freely given. Both traditions connect the burnt offering with the call to offer oneself to God (Romans 12:1).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the burnt offering as symbolizing complete consecration, with atonement in view (Leviticus 1:4). Shared ground: the whole offering belongs to God, and both traditions see it fulfilled in Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice (Hebrews 10:10).

verses.text: one male goat for a sin offering;
verses.arminianNotes: A male goat is the sin offering, matching the offering prescribed for a leader’s sin (Leviticus 4:22–23). Arminian readers see that even leaders need atonement. Both traditions agree that dedication begins with dealing with sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the sin offering as purification required before fellowship with a holy God. Shared ground: leaders are not exempt, and both traditions see the sin offering fulfilled in Christ (Hebrews 9:26; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

verses.text: and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two head of cattle, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Nahshon the son of Amminadab.
verses.arminianNotes: The peace offerings (two cattle, five rams, five goats, five lambs) are the largest part of the gift. Part was eaten by the worshipers (Leviticus 7:15), so the dedication ends in shared fellowship. Arminian readers see joyful communion. This closes Nahshon’s offering.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the peace offering as celebrating restored fellowship after atonement. Both traditions see Christ as the one who makes peace (Ephesians 2:14). Shared ground: the closing formula names Nahshon, honoring his gift individually.

verses.text: On the second day Nethanel the son of Zuar, prince of Issachar, gave his offering.
verses.arminianNotes: Issachar offers on the second day, camped beside Judah on the east (Numbers 2:5). Arminian readers note that a less prominent tribe gives exactly what Judah gave. Both traditions agree that the order follows the camp arrangement, not rank of worth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the equal treatment of Issachar as a sign that standing before God’s altar does not depend on tribal prominence. Shared ground: Nethanel’s gift matches Nahshon’s, and each tribe is honored alike.

verses.text: He offered for his offering: one silver platter, the weight of which was one hundred thirty shekels, one silver bowl of seventy shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a meal offering;
verses.arminianNotes: Issachar’s silver vessels and grain offering exactly match Judah’s. Arminian readers see willing participation that does not try to outdo or underdo the others. Both traditions agree that the meal offering expresses dedication of daily provision to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the meal offering as acknowledging that daily bread comes from God. The identical weights stress equality. Shared ground: the flour and oil are gifts of ordinary life offered to the LORD.

verses.text: one golden ladle of ten shekels, full of incense;
verses.arminianNotes: Issachar’s gold ladle of incense matches Judah’s. Arminian readers see equal access to the worship that incense represents. Both traditions note the connection between incense and the prayers of God’s people (Revelation 5:8).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the gold ladle as a reminder that worship is costly and holy, offered with what is precious. Shared ground: incense pictures prayer, and Issachar brings exactly the same offering of devotion as Judah.

verses.text: one young bull, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering;
verses.arminianNotes: Issachar’s burnt offering of bull, ram, and lamb matches Judah’s. Arminian readers see equal devotion from each tribe. Both traditions agree that the burnt offering expresses complete dedication to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the burnt offering was accepted to make atonement for the worshiper (Leviticus 1:4), so dedication and atonement are intertwined. Shared ground: the whole animal is given to God, picturing entire devotion.

verses.text: one male goat for a sin offering;
verses.arminianNotes: Issachar’s sin offering of a male goat matches Judah’s. Arminian readers see that all need atonement. Both traditions agree that the sin offering addresses the defilement of sin before worship can proceed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the sin offering as God’s gracious provision, not a human achievement: God himself appoints the means by which sinful people are cleansed. Shared ground: atonement is necessary for approaching God, and Issachar’s leader brings it like Judah’s.

verses.text: and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two head of cattle, five rams, five male goats, five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Nethanel the son of Zuar.
verses.arminianNotes: Issachar’s seventeen animals for peace offerings match Judah’s. Arminian readers see fellowship with God offered to all tribes equally. Both traditions agree that the peace offering expresses communion and joy. The verse closes by naming Nethanel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the peace offering as a covenant meal. Shared ground: the closing formula names the giver, honoring each leader’s gift, and the peace offering celebrates fellowship with God.

verses.text: On the third day Eliab the son of Helon, prince of the children of Zebulun,
verses.arminianNotes: Zebulun, the third tribe of the eastern camp (Numbers 2:7), brings its gift through Eliab. Arminian readers note the steady participation of each tribe in turn. Both traditions agree that the recurring pattern underlines the unity of Israel’s worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Zebulun, like Issachar a son of Leah, receives a full and equal record. Shared ground: the orderly sequence reflects God’s arrangement of the camp around his dwelling.

verses.text: gave his offering: one silver platter, the weight of which was a hundred and thirty shekels, one silver bowl of seventy shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a meal offering;
verses.arminianNotes: Zebulun’s platter and bowl, filled with flour and oil, serve both as gifts to the sanctuary and as vessels for its service. Arminian readers note that the gifts remain in use for worship. Both traditions agree the silver honors God’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that precious metal and simple grain are joined in one offering. Shared ground: the meal offering, described in Leviticus 2, is a gift of thanks and dedication, and the vessels serve the altar’s ongoing worship.

verses.text: one golden ladle of ten shekels, full of incense;
verses.arminianNotes: Zebulun’s gold ladle of incense is small in weight but precious in material. Arminian readers note that devotion is measured by sincerity, not size. Both traditions agree the incense offering represents worship rising before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that gold, the most precious metal, is reserved for objects near God’s presence. Shared ground: the incense offering expresses reverent worship and is presented according to God’s prescription.

verses.text: one young bull, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering;
verses.arminianNotes: Zebulun’s burnt offering repeats the three animals of descending size, from bull to ram to lamb. Arminian readers note the costliness of the gift for a pastoral people. Both traditions agree that the burnt offering signified surrender to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the offering as part of the sacrificial system that pointed forward to Christ. Shared ground: the burnt offering is wholly consumed, and its meaning is complete dedication.

verses.text: one male goat for a sin offering;
verses.arminianNotes: Zebulun’s leader brings the same male goat for a sin offering. Arminian readers see the humble acknowledgment that even a leader’s dedication must begin with confession. Both traditions agree that the sin offering purifies and restores fellowship with God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the sin offering as pointing beyond itself to Christ’s atoning work, since animal blood could not finally remove sin (Hebrews 10:4). Shared ground: no tribe approaches God’s altar without atonement, and Zebulun’s offering says so plainly.

verses.text: and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two head of cattle, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Eliab the son of Helon.
verses.arminianNotes: Zebulun’s peace offerings repeat the pattern. Arminian readers see the joy of fellowship after atonement. Both traditions agree that the peace offering is a shared meal before God. The verse closes by naming Eliab.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the order of offerings, sin and burnt before peace, as teaching that fellowship follows atonement. Shared ground: the peace offering celebrates communion, and the giver is named.

verses.text: On the fourth day Elizur the son of Shedeur, prince of the children of Reuben,
verses.arminianNotes: Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn, offers fourth as head of the southern camp (Numbers 2:10). Arminian readers note that Reuben still serves faithfully though he lost the preeminence (Genesis 49:3–4). Both traditions see God’s order, not birth order, setting the sequence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign ordering, which places Judah before Reuben, consistent with Genesis 49. Yet Reuben’s gift is identical. Shared ground: no tribe is excluded, and each brings the same complete offering.

verses.text: gave his offering: one silver platter, the weight of which was one hundred thirty shekels, one silver bowl of seventy shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a meal offering;
verses.arminianNotes: Reuben’s grain offering in silver vessels shows that the firstborn tribe gives the same as the others. Arminian readers note humility in accepting God’s order. Both traditions agree that the offering’s value is set by God’s standard, the sanctuary shekel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the identical offering as a picture of equal standing under God’s covenant. Shared ground: the meal offering represents dedication of the people’s labor and sustenance to the LORD.

verses.text: one golden ladle of ten shekels, full of incense;
verses.arminianNotes: Reuben’s ladle of incense continues the pattern. Arminian readers see the incense as a picture of prayer offered by each tribe. Both traditions agree that the identical gift reflects equal participation in worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that incense in the sanctuary was accompanied by priestly mediation. Many in both traditions see Christ’s intercession foreshadowed (Hebrews 7:25), though this is a typological reading. Shared ground: prayer rises to God through his appointed means.

verses.text: one young bull, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering;
verses.arminianNotes: Reuben’s burnt offering of bull, ram, and lamb is recorded fully. Arminian readers see willing surrender from the firstborn tribe. Both traditions agree that the burnt offering expressed devotion and dependence on God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the burnt offering as part of God’s provision for approaching him. Shared ground: the whole offering is given to the LORD, and both traditions read it in light of Christ’s sacrifice.

verses.text: one male goat for a sin offering;
verses.arminianNotes: Reuben’s sin offering of a male goat is recorded fully. Arminian readers see that the firstborn tribe also needs atonement. Both traditions agree that the sin offering deals with sin before dedication.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in Reuben’s sin offering a reminder that no human privilege, not even birthright, removes the need for atonement. Shared ground: every tribe, first or last, brings the same sin offering before it brings its peace offerings.

verses.text: and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two head of cattle, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Elizur the son of Shedeur.
verses.arminianNotes: Reuben’s peace offerings are recorded fully. Arminian readers see fellowship extended to the firstborn tribe. Both traditions agree that the peace offering expresses joy and communion. The verse closes by naming Elizur.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the peace offering as celebrating God’s covenant fellowship with a forgiven people, a meal eaten in his presence. Shared ground: the closing formula names Elizur personally, and the peace offering is shared joyfully.

verses.text: On the fifth day Shelumiel the son of Zurishaddai, prince of the children of Simeon,
verses.arminianNotes: Simeon, camped with Reuben on the south (Numbers 2:12), offers fifth through Shelumiel. Arminian readers note that Simeon, rebuked with Levi in Genesis 49:5–7, still participates fully. Both traditions see grace in Simeon’s inclusion at the altar.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Simeon’s earlier history does not bar it from bringing the same gift as the others. Shared ground: God receives each tribe at his altar on equal terms.

verses.text: gave his offering: one silver platter, the weight of which was one hundred thirty shekels, one silver bowl of seventy shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a meal offering;
verses.arminianNotes: Simeon’s offering repeats the silver platter and bowl with flour and oil. Arminian readers see consistency in devotion, each tribe bringing its full share. Both traditions note that the oil mixed with flour follows the meal offering instructions of Leviticus 2:1–4.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the repetition highlights faithful conformity to the pattern. Shared ground: the grain offering expresses gratitude and dedication, and both traditions see the whole system fulfilled in Christ’s offering of himself (Hebrews 10:10).

verses.text: one golden ladle of ten shekels, full of incense;
verses.arminianNotes: Simeon’s gold ladle full of incense is recorded identically. Arminian readers see consistent devotion across the tribes. Both traditions agree that incense was a fragrant offering signifying worship acceptable to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the incense as part of worship ordered by God, offered in prescribed vessels and at prescribed times. Shared ground: the ladle and incense honor God, express the people’s prayers, and come from Simeon on equal terms.

verses.text: one young bull, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering;
verses.arminianNotes: Simeon’s burnt offering matches the others. Arminian readers note that the year-old lamb recalls Passover. Many in both traditions see Christ as the Lamb foreshadowed in such offerings (John 1:29), a typological reading.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the burnt offering as pointing to Christ’s complete self-offering. Shared ground: the burnt offering expresses entire devotion to God, and it belongs to the system fulfilled in Christ.

verses.text: one male goat for a sin offering;
verses.arminianNotes: Simeon’s male goat for a sin offering matches the others. Arminian readers see that God provides atonement for every tribe without exception, including one with a troubled past. Both traditions agree that the sin offering is a gracious provision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the sin offering as part of the sacrificial system fulfilled in Christ, who suffered outside the gate (Hebrews 13:11–12). Shared ground: atonement is necessary and provided by God.

verses.text: and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two head of cattle, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old: this was the offering of Shelumiel the son of Zurishaddai.
verses.arminianNotes: Simeon’s seventeen animals for peace offerings match the others. Arminian readers see fellowship with God offered freely to every tribe. Both traditions agree that the peace offering celebrates communion and joy. The verse closes by naming Shelumiel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the peace offering as a covenant meal in which God’s people eat in his presence after atonement has been made. Shared ground: the giver is named, and the peace offering celebrates fellowship with God.

verses.text: On the sixth day, Eliasaph the son of Deuel, prince of the children of Gad,
verses.arminianNotes: Gad, the third tribe of the southern camp, offers through Eliasaph. Numbers 1:14 also reads Deuel, while the WEB of 2:14 reads Reuel, likely a spelling difference between similar Hebrew letters. Arminian readers note Gad’s equal place in worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Gad, a son of Leah’s servant Zilpah, receives the same honor as Leah’s sons. Shared ground: the record makes no distinction by mother or rank, and the first six days close with Gad’s identical gift.

verses.text: gave his offering: one silver platter, the weight of which was one hundred thirty shekels, one silver bowl of seventy shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a meal offering;
verses.arminianNotes: Gad’s silver vessels with flour and oil complete the first six days’ meal offerings. Arminian readers note the steady generosity of the tribes. Both traditions agree that grain offerings accompanied other sacrifices as tokens of dedication.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the meal offering as part of a complete act of worship. Shared ground: the people’s gifts serve God’s altar, and the identical record shows that God values each tribe’s devotion equally.

verses.text: one golden ladle of ten shekels, full of incense;
verses.arminianNotes: Gad’s ladle of incense completes the first half of the list. Arminian readers note that each tribe joins in the same act of devotion. Both traditions agree that incense pictures prayer and worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repetition as reinforcing the orderliness of worship, in which nothing is improvised. Shared ground: incense belongs to the holy service of God, and Gad’s gift is accepted exactly as Judah’s was.

verses.text: one young bull, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering;
verses.arminianNotes: Gad’s burnt offering completes the first six days of burnt offerings. Arminian readers see devotion offered consistently, day after day. Both traditions agree that the three animals together form a costly and complete burnt offering.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the offering as an act of worship ordered by God’s law and repeated faithfully. Shared ground: the whole burnt offering belongs to God, symbolizes complete dedication, and anticipates Christ’s self-offering.

verses.text: one male goat for a sin offering;
verses.arminianNotes: Gad’s sin offering completes the first half of the list. Arminian readers see humility repeated in each tribe’s acknowledgment of sin, a reminder that confession is never finished business. Both traditions agree that the sin offering purifies the worshiper.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the sin offering as an expression of both God’s holiness, which requires atonement, and his grace, which provides it. Shared ground: dedication requires atonement, and the sixth day’s offering repeats that lesson.

verses.text: and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two head of cattle, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Eliasaph the son of Deuel.
verses.arminianNotes: Gad’s peace offerings complete the first half. Arminian readers see joy and fellowship. Both traditions agree that the peace offering expresses communion with God. The verse closes by naming Eliasaph.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the peace offering as pointing to the peace Christ makes through the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). Shared ground: Eliasaph is named personally, and fellowship with God is celebrated.
